steps.title: Ten Moves, Three Jobs
steps.text:
Both sides have a pawn in the middle and everything else at home. From here, about ten moves settle the shape of the game — the time it takes to finish three jobs.

1. **Claim a share of the center.** A pawn in the middle holds squares your pieces want.
2. **Bring out a new piece every move.** Knights and bishops first; they reach work in one hop.
3. **Put the king in a corner.** A king still in the middle when lines open is a target, not a piece.

Whoever finishes first attacks while the other side is still tidying up.

steps.title: What a Move Buys
steps.text:
{{Nf3}} {{Nc6}}. Two knights off the back rank, both pointing at the center, and neither needs to move again to be doing something.

That is **development** — a piece that has left home and already has a job. The thing you spend on it has a name too: a **tempo** is one move, one turn. You get one per turn and so does your opponent.

So a piece moved twice in the opening has cost two tempi and done the work of one. The whole opening is an argument over that arithmetic.

steps.prompt: Develop a bishop so that it aims straight at the one square in Black's camp the king defends alone.
steps.hint: Your king's bishop has five squares on its road out, and only one of them aims at that soft pawn.

steps.title: The Queen Is Not Developed
steps.text:
Black played the queen out on move two, and it is the only black piece off the back rank. Fastest development of the game, on paper.

On the board it is the slowest. A piece is developed when the opponent cannot chase it for free, and the queen is the one piece anyone can chase — a knight, a bishop, even a pawn. Nine points has to run from three. The attacker stays where it landed and keeps the square it just took.

Every one of those chases is a tempo Black hands over.

steps.prompt: Bring a knight out to a square where it attacks the black queen, gaining a move while you develop.
steps.hint: Two knights, five squares between them, and only one of those squares looks at d5.

steps.title: Counting the Bill
steps.text:
The queen has to answer your knight, and answering is all Black gets to do. {{Qa5}} steps out of the way. {{d4}} plants a pawn in the middle while the queen is busy. {{Nf6}} is the first black piece to reach a square it wants, and it arrives on move four.

Count what each side owns. White: a knight on c3, a pawn on d4, and the say in what happens next. Black: one knight, and a queen that can still be chased. Holding that say is **the initiative**.

> A queen that keeps running is buying the other side free moves.

steps.title: Two Moves in One Turn
steps.text:
Look at what is unfinished. White has a pawn on e4, a bishop on c4 and a knight on f3 out; the king is still on e1, and the rook on h1 has never had a square to go to.

One turn fixes both. The king travels two squares toward the corner and the rook hops over it onto f1 — the king now behind three pawns that have never moved, the rook now on a file where it has something to do.

Black's king is on that same middle file, and White moves first.

steps.prompt: Finish the last of the three jobs in a single move, and let the rook in the corner join in.
steps.hint: Two jobs are already done on this board: a pawn in the center, two pieces out. The third one is about your king.
